statements.claim: Every street of Hastinapura was adorned as though for a festival when Krishna came; the principal avenues were decorated with jewels and gems, and no one, man, woman or child, remained indoors, so eager were the citizens to see him.
statements.evidence: MBh 5.089: 'in honour of Krishna, the city was beautifully adorned, and the principal streets were decorated with diverse jewels and gems. And, O king, ... on that occasion no one,--man, woman, or child,--remained in doors, so eager were the citizens for beholding Vasudeva.'

statements.claim: Before he reached the gates the welcome had begun: all the Dhartarashtras except Duryodhana, attired in their finest robes, had gone out to meet him together with Bhishma, Drona, Kripa and the other elders, and the people followed by thousands, on cars of diverse kinds and many on foot.
statements.evidence: MBh 5.089: 'And all the Dhartarashtras except Duryodhana, attired in excellent robes, and with Bhishma, Drona, Kripa, and others, went out to meet him. And the citizens by thousands, O king, on cars of diverse kinds, and many on foot, also came out, desirous of beholding Hrishikesa.'

statements.claim: Krishna had risen at day-dawn, gone through his morning rites, and taken leave of the Bharatas before setting out for the city of the Kurus; the inhabitants of Vrikasthala came out to bid him farewell and only returned to their homes when he was gone.
statements.evidence: MBh 5.089: 'Rising up (from his bed) at day-dawn, Krishna went through his morning rites, and taking leave of the Bharatas, set out for the city (of the Kurus). And all the inhabitants of Vrikasthala, bidding farewell unto that mighty one of long arms while he was about to depart, all returned to their homes.'

statements.claim: Meeting Bhishma of spotless deed, Drona and Dhritarashtra's sons on the way, Krishna entered the city surrounded by them all; citizens lined the streets, bent their heads down to the ground and sang eulogies in his honour as he passed through.
statements.evidence: MBh 5.089: 'meeting on the way Bhishma of spotless deed, and Drona, and Dhritarashtra's sons, he entered the city, surrounded by them all... And all the citizens came out and lined the streets and bent their heads down to the ground singing eulogies in his honour.'

statements.claim: Substantial mansions, filled with high-born ladies, seemed about to fall down under their living weight, and Krishna's steeds, endued with great speed, moved very slowly through that dense mass of human beings.
statements.evidence: MBh 5.089: 'substantial mansions, filled with high-born ladies, seemed to be on the point of falling down on the ground in consequence of their living weight. And although Vasudeva's steeds were endued with great speed, yet they moved very slowly through that dense mass of human beings.' The women leaning thickly from the windows is a light visual elaboration of this, not contradicted by the pack.

statements.claim: Krishna came at last to Dhritarashtra's ash-coloured palace, enriched with numerous buildings, passed through the first three chambers, and came upon the royal son of Vichitravirya, the blind king Dhritarashtra.
statements.evidence: MBh 5.089: 'that lotus-eyed grinder of foes then entered Dhritarashtra's ash-coloured palace which was enriched with numerous buildings. And having passed through the first three chambers of the palace... Kesava, came upon the royal son of Vichitravirya.'

statements.claim: At Krishna's approach the blind monarch of great fame stood up, and with him rose Drona and Bhishma, Kripa and Somadatta, and king Vahlika also — all of them stood up to honour him.
statements.evidence: MBh 5.089: 'the blind monarch of great fame stood up along with Drona and Bhishma, Kripa and Somadatta, and king Vahlika also,--all stood up for honouring Janardana.'

statements.claim: Krishna worshipped Dhritarashtra and Bhishma with proper words and without losing any time, then greeted the other kings according to their seniority in years and accosted Drona and his son, Vahlika, Kripa and Somadatta.
statements.evidence: MBh 5.089: 'the Vrishni hero... worshipped him and Bhishma with proper words and without losing any time... greeted the other kings according to their seniority in years. And Janardana then accosted the illustrious Drona and his son, and Vahlika, and Kripa, and Somadatta.'

statements.claim: In the chamber lay a spacious seat of beautiful workmanship, made of gold and set with jewels; at Dhritarashtra's request Krishna took it, and the king's priests duly offered him a cow, honey and curds and water.
statements.evidence: MBh 5.089: 'there in that chamber lay a spacious seat of beautiful workmanship, made of gold and set with jewels. And at Dhritarashtra's request, Achyuta took that seat; and the priests of Dhritarashtra duly offered Janardana a cow, honey and curds and water.'

statements.claim: After the rites of hospitality Krishna remained a while among the Kurus, laughing and jesting with them according to his relationship with each, and came out with the king's permission; having duly greeted all the Kurus in their assembly, he went to the delightful abode of Vidura, who worshipped him with every auspicious and desirable offering.
statements.evidence: MBh 5.089: 'Govinda remained there for a while, surrounded by the Kurus, laughing and jesting with them according to their relationship with him... came out with the king's permission. And Madhava having duly greeted all the Kurus in their assembly, then went to the delightful abode of Vidura; and Vidura... worshipped him with every auspicious and desirable offering.'

statements.claim: Vidura asked what use in telling Krishna of the joy he felt at this advent, for Krishna was the inner Soul of all embodied creatures; when the reception was over he enquired about the welfare of the Pandavas, and Krishna, to whom the past and the future were as the present, told him everything in detail about the doings of the sons of Pandu.
statements.evidence: MBh 5.089: Vidura's words 'for thou art the inner Soul of all embodied creatures'; 'after the hospitable reception was over, Vidura... enquired of Govinda... about the welfare of Pandavas'; 'that scion of Dasarha's race... unto whom the past and the future were as the present... began to tell him everything in detail about the doings of the sons of Pandu.'

statements.claim: Closing frame: the day that began with the whole city pouring out of doors to see Krishna ended with him speaking of his cousins in the lamplight of Vidura's quiet house, while the errand of peace still waited to be spoken aloud.
statements.evidence: Atmospheric summary of 5.089's own sequence (street welcome → palace → Vidura's abode, where he reports on the Pandavas); no new sourceable fact asserted.

notes: Entire story closely follows MBh 5.089. Story title/summary and the 'women leaning from windows' flourish are visual elaboration consistent with the 'living weight' detail.

statements.claim: After his meeting with Vidura, Krishna went in the afternoon to his paternal aunt Pritha (Kunti), whose countenance... he had not seen in a long time; beholding him, whose countenance beamed like the radiant sun, she encircled his neck with her arms and poured forth lamentations remembering her sons, and the tears of Pritha flowed fast.
statements.evidence: MBh 5.090: 'Janardana... after his meeting with Vidura, went then in the afternoon to his paternal aunt, Pritha. And beholding Krishna whose countenance beamed with the effulgence of the radiant sun arrived at her abode, she encircled his neck with her arms and began to pour forth her lamentations remembering her sons... the tears of Pritha flowed fast.'

statements.claim: Krishna received the rites of hospitality and took his seat, and only then did Kunti speak, with a woe-begone face and a voice choked with tears.
statements.evidence: MBh 5.090: 'after Krishna... had taken his seat having first received the rites of hospitality, Pritha, with a woe-begone face and voice choked with tears addressed him.'

statements.claim: Kunti's sons, she said, had from their earliest years always waited with reverence on their superiors, were attached to one another in friendship, were deprived deceitfully of their kingdom though worthy of living amid friends and attendants, had subjugated both wrath and joy, and were devoted to Brahmans and truthful in speech.
statements.evidence: MBh 5.090: 'They, who, from their earliest years have always waited with reverence on their superiors; they, who, in friendship are attached to one another; they, who, deprived deceitfully of their kingdom had gone to seclusion, however worthy of living in the midst of friends and attendants,--they, who have subjugated both wrath and joy, are devoted to Brahmans, and truthful in speech.'

statements.claim: Those children of hers, who abandoned kingdom and enjoyments, leaving their miserable mother behind, and went to the woods, plucking the very roots of her heart, lived — she asked — in the deep forest abounding with lions and tigers and elephants.
statements.evidence: MBh 5.090: 'those children of mine, who, abandoning kingdom and enjoyments and leaving my miserable self behind, had gone to the woods, plucking the very roots of my heart... how, alas, did they live in the deep forest abounding with lions and tigers and elephants?'

statements.claim: They had been deprived of their father in infancy and brought up tenderly by her; at home they slept in high palatial chambers on soft blankets and the skins of the Runku deer, waked by the grunt of elephants, the neighing of steeds, the clatter of car-wheels and the music of conchs and cymbals, with flutes and lyres, the honeyed strains of songstresses and eulogies chanted by bards and reciters, blessed at early dawn by the sacred hymns of Brahmans.
statements.evidence: MBh 5.090: 'Deprived in their infancy of their father, they were all tenderly brought up by me... who while at home, used to sleep in high palatial chambers on soft blankets and skins of the Runku deer and were waked up in the morning by the grunt of elephants, the neighing of steeds, the clatter of car-wheels and the music of conchs and cymbals in accompaniment with the notes of flutes and lyres... adored at early dawn with sacred sounding hymns uttered by Brahmanas... roused from their beds by music of cymbals and drums and conchs and flutes, with the honeyed strains of songstresses and the eulogies chanted by bards and professional reciters.'

statements.claim: That such sons should sleep in the deep woods resounding with the shrill and dissonant cries of beasts of prey could hardly be believed; those roused from their beds by music and eulogies could not be waked in the wild by the yells of beasts.
statements.evidence: MBh 5.090: 'that they, O Janardana, could sleep in the deep woods resounding with the shrill and dissonant cries of beasts of prey can hardly be believed... how could they be waked in the deep woods by the yells of wild beasts?'

statements.claim: One by one she asked after her sons: Yudhishthira of virtuous soul and complexion like pure gold, foremost of the Kurus, bearer of burdens like the royal sages of old, fit to be monarch of the three worlds; Bhimasena of the strength of ten thousand elephants and speed of the wind, slayer of Hidimva and Vaka and of Kichaka with all his relatives, obedient to his elder brother; and Arjuna, who shot five hundred arrows at one stretch, equal to Kartavirya in weapons, to the sun in energy, to a sage in restraint, to the Earth in forgiveness and to Indra in prowess.
statements.evidence: MBh 5.090: the pack passage details all three in matching terms — Yudhishthira 'of complexion like that of pure gold... able bore the heavy burthen borne by Amvarisha and Mandhatri, Yayati and Nahusha and Bharata and Dilip and Sivi...' 'fit to become the monarch of the three worlds'; Bhimasena 'hath the strength of ten thousand elephants and the speed of the wind... slew Kichaka with all his relatives... slayer of the Krodhavasas, of Hidimva, and of Vaka... obedient to the commands of his elder brother'; Arjuna 'who at one stretch shooteth five hundred arrows... in the use of weapons is equal unto king Kartavirya, in energy unto Aditya, in restraint of senses unto a great sage, in forgiveness unto the Earth, and in prowess unto Indra himself.'

statements.claim: Krishna answered: 'What woman is there in the world who is like thee?' Endued with every virtue and great wisdom, it behooved her to bear with patience both happiness and misery; the Pandavas with Krishna saluted her through him, and she would soon behold them become lords of the whole world, with their foe slain and themselves invested with prosperity.
statements.evidence: Pack excerpt (5.090): 'What woman is there, O aunt, in the world who is like thee?... Endued with every virtue, and endued with great wisdom, it behoveth thee to bear with patience, both happiness and misery... The Pandavas with Krishna saluteth thee through me... Thou wilt soon behold them become the lords of the whole world, with their foe slain, and themselves invested with prosperity.'

statements.claim: Closing frame: Kunti poured out her sorrow to the one person who could answer it as a promise, and let her tears fall knowing her sons would come back to her.
statements.evidence: Non-factual emotional summation of Krishna's reassurance in 5.090; asserts no new sourceable event.

notes: Story mirrors 5.090's lament and Krishna's reply. The pack passage is truncated mid-way (after Arjuna's praises) but the excerpt covers Krishna's consolation verbatim. No unsupported or contradicted claims.

statements.claim: With Pritha's leave and having walked round her in farewell, Krishna went to Duryodhana's palace, furnished with great wealth, adorned with beautiful seats and like unto the abode of Indra himself; unhindered by the orderlies-in-waiting, he crossed three spacious yards and entered the mansion looking like a mass of clouds, high as the summit of a hill and blazing forth in splendour.
statements.evidence: MBh 5.091: 'With Pritha's leave and having walked round her... went to Duryodhana's palace that was furnished with great wealth, adorned with beautiful seats, and was like unto the abode of Purandara himself. Unobstructed by the orderlies-in-waiting... crossed three spacious yards in succession and then entered that mansion looking like a mass of clouds, high as the summit of a hill, and blazing forth in splendour.'

statements.claim: There, in the midst of a thousand kings and surrounded by all the Kurus, sat Dhritarashtra's son of mighty arms on his throne, with Dussasana and Karna and Sakuni, the son of Suvala, seated beside him.
statements.evidence: MBh 5.091: 'he there beheld Dhritarashtra's son of mighty arms seated on his throne in the midst of a thousand kings and surrounded by all the Kurus. And he also beheld there Dussasana and Karna and Sakuni, the son of Suvala, seated on their respective seats by the side of Duryodhana.'

statements.claim: At Krishna's entry Duryodhana rose from his seat with his counsellors to honour him; Krishna greeted Dhritarashtra's sons, all his counsellors and every king present according to their respective ages, and took his seat on a beautiful throne of gold overlaid with a carpet embroidered with gold.
statements.evidence: MBh 5.091: 'Dhritarashtra's son of great fame rose up from his seat with his counsellors for honouring the slayer of Madhu. And Kesava then greeted Dhritarashtra's sons and all his counsellors as also all the kings that were present there, according to their respective ages. And Achyuta of Vrishni's race then took his seat on a beautiful seat made of gold and overlaid with carpet embroidered with gold.'

statements.claim: The Kuru king offered Krishna a cow, and honey and curds and water, placed at his service palaces and mansions and the whole kingdom; and the Kauravas, with all the kings there present, worshipped him as he sat resembling the sun itself in splendour.
statements.evidence: MBh 5.091: 'the Kuru king then offered unto Janardana a cow, and honey and curds and water, and placed at his service palaces and mansions and the whole kingdom. And then the Kauravas, with all the kings there present, worshipped Govinda on his seat and resembling the sun himself in splendour.'

statements.claim: The worship being over, king Duryodhana invited Krishna to eat at his house, but Krishna did not accept the invitation.
statements.evidence: MBh 5.091: 'The worship being over, king Duryodhana invited him of Vrishni's race--that foremost of victors--to eat at his house. Kesava, however did not accept the invitation.'

statements.claim: Duryodhana pressed him in a gentle voice with deception lurking behind his words, eyeing Karna: why would Janardana not accept the viands and drinks, robes and beds prepared and kept ready for him? He had granted aid to both sides, was engaged in the good of both parties, was the foremost of Dhritarashtra's relations and much loved by him; he desired to hear the true reason of the refusal.
statements.evidence: MBh 5.091: 'The Kuru king Duryodhana seated in the midst of the Kurus, in a gentle voice but with deception lurking behind his words, eyeing Karna... said, Why, O Janardana, dost thou not accept the diverse kinds of viands and drinks, robes and beds that have all been prepared and kept ready for thee? Thou hast granted aid to both sides; thou art engaged in the good of both parties. Thou art again the foremost of Dhritarashtra's relations and much loved by him... what the true reason is of this thy refusal.'

statements.claim: Krishna raised his mighty right arm and, in a voice deep as the clouds, replied in words clear and distinct and without a single letter dropped that envoys eat and accept worship only after the success of their missions, so Duryodhana might entertain him and his attendants after his mission became successful.
statements.evidence: MBh 5.091: 'raising his mighty (right) arm, and in a voice deep as that of the clouds, replied unto the king in excellent words fraught with reasons,--words that were clear, distinct, correctly pronounced, and without a single letter dropped, saying, Envoys, O king, eat and accept worship only after the success of their missions. Therefore, O Bharata, after my mission becomes successful, thou mayest entertain me and my attendants.'

statements.claim: Duryodhana answered that it behooved Krishna not to behave so: whether successful or unsuccessful, they were endeavouring to please him because of his relationship with them; with Krishna they had no hostility, no war, and on reflection such words scarcely became him.
statements.evidence: MBh 5.091: 'It behoveth thee not, O Kesava, to behave towards us in this way. Whether thou becomest successful, or unsuccessful, we are endeavouring to please thee... because of thy relationship with us... With thee, O Govinda, we have no hostility, no war. Therefore, on reflection, it will seem to thee that words such as these scarcely become thee.'

statements.claim: Krishna said he would not abandon virtue from desire, wrath, malice, gain, argument or temptation; one takes another's food only when in distress, and Duryodhana had not inspired love in him nor had Krishna been plunged into distress; without any reason the king hated from their very birth his dear and gentle brothers the Pandavas, endued with every virtue — an unreasonable hatred that ill became him; he who hates them hates Krishna and he who loves them loves him, for the virtuous Pandavas and Krishna have but a common soul; and the food of that house, defiled by wickedness, did not deserve to be eaten, whereas the food supplied by Vidura alone should be eaten by him.
statements.evidence: MBh 5.091: 'Not from desire, nor from wrath, nor from malice, nor for gain, nor for the sake of argument, nor from temptation, would I abandon virtue. One taketh another's food when one is in distress... thou hast not inspired love in me by any act of thine, nor have I myself been plunged into distress. Without any reason, O king, thou hatest, from the moment of their birth, thy dear and gentle brothers,--the Pandavas--endued with every virtue... He that hateth them, hateth me; he that loveth them, loveth me. Know that the virtuous Pandavas and my own self have but a common soul.' Food line confirmed by pack excerpt: 'Defiled by wickedness, all this food, therefore, deserveth not to be eaten by me. The food supplied by Vidura alone, should, I think, be eaten by me.'

statements.claim: Closing frame: in a palace furnished for a thousand kings Krishna chose the table of a minister's house; the refusal was not discourtesy but a line drawn — a friend of the Pandavas could not sit at the table of the man who had spent his life hating them.
statements.evidence: Interpretive gloss on the refusal already grounded in 5.091's 'food supplied by Vidura alone should be eaten by me'; no new factual assertion.

notes: All events and speeches track MBh 5.091 near-verbatim (including Krishna's declaration that only Vidura's food should be eaten, which the pack excerpt confirms though the main passage is truncated).

statements.claim: It was at Vidura's table that Krishna had eaten that day (as he had told Duryodhana's court he would); after Krishna had dined and been refreshed, Vidura spoke to him during the night.
statements.evidence: MBh 5.092 opens: 'After Kesava had dined and been refreshed, Vidura said unto him during the night...'; the Vidura-table meal follows from Krishna's own declaration in 5.091 ('The food supplied by Vidura alone, should... be eaten by me.').

statements.claim: Vidura said Krishna's advent had not been a well-judged one: Dhritarashtra's son transgresses the rules of both profit and religion, is wicked and wrathful, insults others though himself desirous of honours, disobeys the commands of the aged, is a transgressor of the scriptures, ignorant and of wicked soul, already overtaken by fate, untractable, disposed to do evil to those who seek his good, his soul possessed by desire and lust, foolishly regarding himself as very wise.
statements.evidence: MBh 5.092: 'this advent of thine hath not been a well judged one, for... Dhritarashtra's son transgresseth the rules of both profit and religion, is wicked and wrathful, insulteth others, though himself desirous of honours, and disobeyeth the commands of the aged. He is... a transgressor of the scriptures, ignorant, and of wicked soul, already overtaken by fate, untractable, and disposed to do evil to those that seek his good. His soul is possessed by desire and lust. He foolishly regardeth himself as very wise.'

statements.claim: Vidura continued the catalogue: Duryodhana is the enemy of all his true friends, ever-suspicious, without control over his soul, ungrateful, has abandoned all virtue and is in love with sin, a slave of his senses, obedient to the impulses of lust and avarice, irresolute in every act that should be done, and endued with many other vices; although Krishna would point out his good, he would disregard it all, moved by pride and anger.
statements.evidence: MBh 5.092: 'He is the enemy of all his true friends. Ever-suspicious, without any control over his soul, and ungrateful, he hath abandoned all virtue and is in love with sin. He is foolish... a slave of his senses, ever obedient to the impulses of lust and avarice, and irresolute in every act that should be done. He is endued with these and many other vices. Although thou wilt point out to him what is for his good, he will yet disregard it all, moved by pride and anger.'

statements.claim: He has great faith in Bhishma, Drona, Kripa, Karna, Drona's son and Jayadratha, and therefore never sets his heart on peace.
statements.evidence: MBh 5.092: 'He hath great faith in Bhishma, and Drona, and Kripa, and Karna, and Drona's son, and Jayadratha, and, therefore, he never setteth his heart on peace.'

statements.claim: Dhritarashtra's sons, with Karna, firmly believed the Pandavas incapable of even looking at Bhishma and Drona, not to speak of fighting them; the foolish Duryodhana of limited sight, having assembled a huge army, regarded his purposes as already achieved and had concluded that Karna single-handed was competent to vanquish his foes; he would therefore never make peace.
statements.evidence: MBh 5.092: 'Dhritarashtra's sons, with Karna, firmly believe that the Pandavas are incapable of even looking at Bhishma, Drona, and other heroes, not to speak of fighting against them. The foolish Duryodhana of limited sight, having assembled a huge army regardeth... that his purposes are already achieved. The foolish son of Dhritarashtra hath arrived at the conclusion that Karna, single-handed, is competent to vanquish his foes. He will, therefore, never make peace.'

statements.claim: Krishna desired to establish peace and brotherly feelings between the two parties, but all the sons of Dhritarashtra had concluded they would not give the Pandavas what they had a right to; with those so resolved his words would certainly prove vain, and as a Brahmana before a conclave of Chandalas his words would command no respect among those ignorant and wicked wretches.
statements.evidence: MBh 5.092: 'Thou, O Kesava, desirest to establish peace and brotherly feelings between the two parties. But know that all the sons of Dhritarashtra have come to the conclusion that they would not give unto the Pandavas what, indeed, the latter have a right to. With those that are so resolved thy words will certainly prove vain... As a Brahmana before a conclave of Chandalas, thy words, O Madhava, would command no respect among those ignorant and wicked wretches that have no reverence for all that deserveth reverence.'

statements.claim: It did not seem proper to Vidura that Krishna should go into the midst of those wicked-minded wretches and utter words against them, for they had mustered a strong force, had suspicions of Krishna himself, and were inspired with the firm belief that Indra at the head of all the celestials was incapable of defeating them in battle.
statements.evidence: MBh 5.092: 'It doth not seem proper to me, O Krishna, that thou shouldst go into the midst of these wicked-minded wretches seated together... He hath mustered a strong force, O Madhava, and he hath his suspicions of thyself... The sons of Dhritarashtra, O Janardana, are inspired with the firm belief that at present Indra himself, at the head of all the celestials, is incapable of defeating them in battle.'

statements.claim: Staying in the midst of his ranks of elephants and his army of cars and heroic infantry, the foolish and wicked Duryodhana, with all fears dispelled, regarded the whole earth as already subjugated and coveted extensive empire without rivals, so peace with him was unattainable; what he possesses he regards as unalterably his, and the destruction of the earth seemed at hand for his sake, with all the kings and Kshatriya warriors assembled, desirous of battling with the Pandavas.
statements.evidence: MBh 5.092: 'Staying in the midst of his ranks of elephants and his army consisting of cars and heroic infantry, the foolish and wicked Duryodhana, with all fears dispelled, regardeth the whole earth to have already been subjugated by him... coveteth extensive empire on the earth without any rivals. Peace, therefore, with him is unattainable. That which he hath in his possession he regardeth as unalterably his. Alas, the destruction on the earth seems to be at hand for the sake of Duryodhana... the kings of the earth, with all the Kshatriya warriors, have assembled together, desirous of battling with the Pandavas.'

statements.claim: All those kings are in enmity with Krishna and had been deprived of their possessions before this by him; through fear of him they joined with Karna and allied with Dhritarashtra's sons, and reckless of their very lives they united with Duryodhana, filled with delight at the prospect of fighting the Pandavas; Vidura did not commend it that Krishna should enter their midst.
statements.evidence: MBh 5.092: 'All those kings, O Krishna, are in enmity with thee and have all been deprived of their possessions before this by thee. Through fear of thee those heroic monarchs have joined together with Karna and made an alliance with Dhritarashtra's sons. Reckless of their very lives, all those warriors have united with Duryodhana and are filled with delight at the prospect of fighting the Pandavas... it doth not commend itself to me that thou shouldst enter into their midst.'

statements.claim: Closing frame: Krishna heard every word — the catalogue of Duryodhana's vices, the certainty of war, the plea that he not walk into that assembly — and did not argue with any of it; he had not come to Hastinapura to be persuaded out of listening.
statements.evidence: Non-factual staging of Vidura's night-long warning (5.092); consistent with 5.093, where Krishna answers the warning rather than disputing it.

notes: Faithful rendering of Vidura's night warning in MBh 5.092. All descriptive epithets and arguments match the passage.

statements.claim: Setting recap: in Vidura's house by night Krishna, come as a messenger of peace, had just heard Vidura spell out Duryodhana's wickedness and the hostility of the Kshatriyas who sided with him.
statements.evidence: Frame linking to the preceding night scene (5.092, Vidura's warning); consistent with 5.093 where Krishna responds to exactly that warning. No new sourceable fact.

statements.claim: Krishna told Vidura everything he had said was true, worthy of him, consistent with virtue and profit and truth, spoken as a father and mother would speak.
statements.evidence: MBh 5.093: 'that... which is deserving of thee, being consistent with virtue and profit, and truth; that, O Vidura, hath been said by thee, father and mother-like, unto me... That which thou hast told me is certainly true, worthy of approbation and consistent with reason.'

statements.claim: Well knowing the wickedness of Dhritarashtra's son and the hostility of the Kshatriyas who had sided with him, Krishna had still come to the Kurus; great would be the merit earned by him who freed the whole earth — with its elephants, chariots and steeds — from the meshes of death, overwhelmed by a dreadful calamity.
statements.evidence: MBh 5.093 (pack excerpt): 'Well knowing the wickedness of Dhritarashtra's son and the hostility of the Kshatriyas that have sided with him, I have still, O Vidura, come to the Kurus. Great will be the merit earned by him who will liberate from the meshes of death the whole earth, with her elephants, cars and steeds, overwhelmed with a dreadful calamity.'

statements.claim: If a man strives with all his might to perform a virtuous act and meets with failure, the merit of that act is still his; and if a person only intends a sinful act in his mind but never commits it, the demerit can never touch him.
statements.evidence: MBh 5.093: 'If a man striving to the best of his abilities to perform a virtuous act meets with failure, I have not the least doubt that the merit of that act becomes his, notwithstanding such failure... if a person having intended mentally to commit a sinful act does not actually commit it, the demerit of that act can never be his.'

statements.claim: Krishna said he would sincerely endeavour to bring about peace between the Kurus and the Srinjayas, who were about to be slaughtered in battle; the terrible calamity over them all had its origin in the conduct of the Kurus, being directly due to the actions of Duryodhana and Karna, the other Kshatriyas only following these two's lead.
statements.evidence: MBh 5.093: 'I will sincerely endeavour, O Vidura, to bring about peace between the Kurus and the Srinjayas who are about to be slaughtered in battle. That terrible calamity (which hangs over them all) hath its origin in the conduct of the Kurus, for it is directly due to the action of Duryodhana and Karna, the other Kshatriyas only following the lead of these two.'

statements.claim: The learned regard as a wretch one who does not by his solicitation seek to save a friend about to sink in calamity; striving with all his might, even to seizing his friend by the hair, one should dissuade him from an improper act, and he who acts so reaps praise, not blame.
statements.evidence: MBh 5.093: 'The learned regard him to be a wretch who doth not by his solicitation seek to save a friend who is about to sink in calamity. Striving to the best of his might, even to the extent of seizing him by the hair, one should seek to dissuade a friend from an improper act. In that case, he that acteth so, instead of incurring blame, reapeth praise.'

statements.claim: A true friend takes on the work of an intercessor when dissension breaks out between kinsmen; if Duryodhana judged him wrongly Krishna would still have the satisfaction of his own conscience.
statements.evidence: MBh 5.093: 'a true friend is one who assumeth the functions of an intercessor when dissensions break out between kinsmen... If while endeavouring to bring about the good (of my friends), Duryodhana judgeth me wrongly, I shall have the satisfaction of my own conscience.'

statements.claim: Krishna had come so that no unrighteous, foolish and inimical person might later say that Krishna, though competent, had made no attempt to restrain the angry Kurus and Pandavas from slaughtering one another; it was to serve both parties that he came, and having striven for peace he would escape the censure of all the kings.
statements.evidence: MBh 5.093: 'In order, again, that unrighteous, foolish, and inimical persons may not afterwards say that though competent, still Krishna did not make any attempt to restrain the angry Kurus and the Pandavas from slaughtering one another I have come here. Indeed, it is to serve both parties that I have come hither. Having striven to bring about peace, I will escape the censure of all the kings.'

statements.claim: If the foolish Duryodhana accepted not his words he would only invite his fate; if Krishna could bring about peace among the Kurus without sacrificing the interests of the Pandavas, his conduct would be highly meritorious and the Kauravas themselves liberated from the meshes of death; if the sons of Dhritarashtra reflected coolly on his words, peace would be brought about and the Kauravas would honour him as its agent.
statements.evidence: MBh 5.093: 'If after listening to my auspicious words... the foolish Duryodhana accept them not, he will only invite his fate. If without sacrificing the interests of the Pandavas I can bring about peace among the Kurus, my conduct will be regarded as highly meritorious... and the Kauravas themselves will be liberated from the meshes of death. If the sons of Dhritarashtra reflect coolly on the words I shall utter... then that peace which is my object will be brought about and the Kauravas will also worship me (as the agent thereof).'

statements.claim: If, on the other hand, they sought to injure him, all the kings of the earth united together were no match for him — like a herd of deer incapable of standing before an enraged lion.
statements.evidence: MBh 5.093: 'If, on the other hand, they seek to injure me, I tell thee that all the kings of the earth united together, are no match for me, like a herd of deer incapable of standing before an enraged lion.'

statements.claim: Having said these words Krishna laid himself down on his soft bed for the night; the story adds that Vidura remained wakeful long after, weighing Krishna's words.
statements.evidence: MBh 5.093 closes: 'Having said these words... then laid himself down on his soft bed for sleep.' Vidura's wakefulness is a connective inference consistent with 5.094's opening, where the night passes in the two men's continued conversation.

statements.claim: Closing frame: the lamps flickered and the city slept on; somewhere between Krishna's plea for peace and his declaration that he could not be harmed lay the whole of what was about to happen to the world.
statements.evidence: Non-factual atmospheric close on 5.093's content; no new claims.

notes: Speech closely follows MBh 5.093, including the notable 'Kurus and the Srinjayas' phrasing and the merit/demerit doctrine. No unsupported claims.

statements.claim: The night passed in talk between Krishna and Vidura, and at early dawn a band of choristers and bards gifted with melodious voices woke Kesava with the sweet sounds of conchs and cymbals at Vidura's house.
statements.evidence: MBh 5.094: 'In such conversation between those two distinguished persons... that night, lit with bright stars, passed away... Then, at early dawn a band of choristers and bards gifted with melodious voices, awoke Kesava with sweet sounds of conchs and cymbals.'

statements.claim: Krishna rose and went through the customary acts of the morning: cleansing by a bath, reciting the sacred mantras, pouring libations of clarified butter on the sacrificial fire, decking his person, and beginning his worship of the rising sun.
statements.evidence: MBh 5.094: 'rising from bed, Janardana... went through all the customary acts of the morning. And having cleansed himself by a bath, recited the sacred Mantras and poured libations of clarified butter on the sacrificial fire, Madhava decked his person and began to worship the rising sun.'

statements.claim: While Krishna was still engaged in his morning devotions, Duryodhana and Sakuni, the son of Suvala, came to him and said Dhritarashtra was seated in his court with all the Kurus headed by Bhishma and all the kings of the earth, all soliciting Krishna's presence like the celestials desiring the presence of Indra himself.
statements.evidence: MBh 5.094: 'while the unvanquished Krishna... was still engaged in his morning devotions, Duryodhana and Suvala's son Sakuni came to him and said, Dhritarashtra is seated in his court, with all the Kurus headed by Bhishma and with all the kings of the earth. They are all soliciting thy presence, O Govinda, like the celestials in heaven desiring the presence of Sakra himself.'

statements.claim: Krishna greeted them both with sweet and courteous enquiries; when the sun had risen a little higher he summoned a number of Brahmanas and made them presents of gold, robes, kine and steeds.
statements.evidence: MBh 5.094: 'Govinda greeted them both with sweet and courteous enquiries. And when the sun had risen a little higher, Janardana... summoning a number of Brahmanas, made them presents of gold and robes and kine and steeds.'

statements.claim: His driver Daruka came and saluted him and soon returned with his master's large and blazing car, furnished with rows of tinkling bells and harnessed with excellent steeds, producing a rattle deep as the rumbling of mighty masses of clouds.
statements.evidence: MBh 5.094: 'his driver (Daruka) came and saluted that unvanquished hero... And Daruka soon returned with his master's large and blazing car furnished with rows of tinkling bells and harnessed with excellent steeds... producing a rattle, deep as the rumbling of the mighty masses of clouds.'

statements.claim: Krishna walked round the sacred fire and a band of Brahmanas, put on the gem known as the Kaustubha, and mounted the car, blazing with beauty, surrounded by the Kurus and well protected by the Vrishnis.
statements.evidence: MBh 5.094: 'the high-souled Janardana... walking round the sacred fire and a band of Brahmanas, and putting on the gem known by the name of Kaustubha, and blazing with beauty, surrounded by the Kurus, and well-protected by the Vrishnis, mounted on it.'

statements.claim: Vidura followed on his own car; Duryodhana and Sakuni followed on one car; and Satyaki, Kritavarman and the other mighty car-warriors of the Vrishni race rode behind on cars, steeds and elephants.
statements.evidence: MBh 5.094: 'And Vidura... followed on his own car... And Duryodhana and Suvala's son Sakuni also on one car followed Krishna... And Satyaki and Kritavarman and the other mighty car-warriors of the Vrishni race, all rode behind Krishna on cars and steeds and elephants.'

statements.claim: Kesava came upon a broad street that had been swept and watered and was fit for the highest of kings; cymbals played, conchs were blown and other instruments poured forth music; youthful heroes of lion-like prowess surrounded Sauri's car; thousands of soldiers in variegated dresses bearing swords, lances and axes marched in advance; full five hundred elephants and chariots by thousands followed.
statements.evidence: MBh 5.094: 'Kesava... soon came upon a broad street that had previously been swept and watered, and that was fit to be used by the highest of kings. And when that scion of Dasarha's race set out, cymbals began to play, and conchs began to be blown... And great number of youthful heroes... possessed of lion-like prowess, proceeded, surrounding Sauri's car. And many thousands of soldiers, attired in a variegated dresses, bearing swords and lances and axes, marched in advance of Kesava. And there were full five hundred elephants, and cars by thousands, that followed.'

statements.claim: All the citizens of the capital, of every age and both sexes, came out into the streets desiring to behold Janardana; terraces and balconies were so thronged by ladies that the houses seemed on the point of falling down with the weight.
statements.evidence: MBh 5.094: 'all the citizens of the capital, of all ages and both sexes, desirous of beholding Janardana came out into the streets. And the terraces and balconies of the houses were so thronged by ladies that the houses were on the point of falling down with the weight.'

statements.claim: Worshipped by the Kurus, listening to sweet speeches and returning the greetings of all as each deserved, Kesava went along the street casting his eyes on all; at the Kuru court his attendants loudly blew conchs and trumpets, filling the sky with the blare, and the whole assembly of kings trembled with delight, their hair standing erect, at the expectation of seeing Krishna.
statements.evidence: MBh 5.094: 'worshipped by the Kurus, and listening to various sweet speeches, and returning the greetings of all as each deserved, Kesava went along the street, casting his eyes on all. And at last, when Kesava reached the Kuru court, his attendants loudly blew their conchs and trumpets and filled the welkin with that blare... that whole assembly of kings... trembled with delight at the expectation of soon setting their eyes on Krishna... the hair of their bodies stood erect with delight.'

statements.claim: At the gate of the court Krishna alighted from his car, which resembled the summit of Kailasa, and entered the court, which looked like a mass of newly risen clouds, blazing with beauty, like the very abode of great Indra; he entered arm-in-arm with Vidura and Satyaki on either side, overshadowing with his own the splendour of all the Kurus.
statements.evidence: MBh 5.094 (pack excerpt): 'Sauri... alighting from his car... entered the court which looked like a mass of newly-risen clouds... And that illustrious hero entered the court, arm-in-arm with Vidura and Satyaki on either side, and overshadowing with his own the splendour of all the Kurus.' Kailasa simile: 'his car, that resembled the summit of Kailasa.'

statements.claim: The kings made way; the Rishis who had come to the assembly were given their seats; and Krishna took his seat in the midst of the assembly.
statements.evidence: Index summary for evt_0433: 'Krishna rides in procession to the Kuru court, enters arm-in-arm with Vidura and Satyaki, and after the Rishis are seated takes his seat in the assembly.' The pack passage continues past the excerpt into the seating of the Rishis (5.094).

statements.claim: Closing frame: Krishna sat, the calm centre of a court that had dressed itself in all its glory to receive him — a glory that seemed borrowed from his presence rather than lent to it.
statements.evidence: Non-factual atmospheric close consistent with the assembly's awe in 5.094 ('hair of their bodies stood erect with delight').

notes: Close verse-by-verse rendering of MBh 5.094 (procession, mount, escort, street, assembly entry). Krishna 'passed the night in talk' matches 5.094's opening, not the sleep-close of 5.093 used in the previous story — each story matches its own pack.

statements.claim: After all the kings had been seated and perfect silence had ensued, Krishna — whose voice was deep as that of the drum and deep as the roll of clouds in the rainy season — addressed Dhritarashtra but spoke so the whole assembly heard him.
statements.evidence: MBh 5.095: 'after all the kings had been seated and perfect silence had ensued, Krishna possessing fine teeth and having a voice deep as that of the drum, began to speak. And Madhava although he addressed Dhritarashtra, spoke in a voice deep as the roll of clouds in the rainy season, making the whole assembly hear.'

statements.claim: Krishna said: 'In order that peace may be established between the Kurus and the Pandavas without a slaughter of the heroes, I have come here. I have no other words to offer, O king. Everything that should be learnt in this world is already known to you.'
statements.evidence: MBh 5.095: 'In order that, O Bharata, peace may be established between the Kurus and the Pandavas without a slaughter of the heroes, I have come hither. Besides this, O king, I have no other beneficial words to utter. O chastiser of foes, everything that should be learnt in this world is already known to thee.'

statements.claim: The Kuru dynasty was distinguished among all royal dynasties for its learning, behaviour and accomplishments, where joy in others' happiness, grief at misery, desire to relieve distress, abstention from injury, sincerity, forgiveness and truth prevailed; it would be a pity if anything improper were done by any of such a race, and a greater pity if done by Dhritarashtra himself, who was first among those who should restrain the Kurus from behaving deceitfully toward strangers or kin.
statements.evidence: MBh 5.095: 'This thy race, O king, owing to its learning and behaviour, and owing also to its being adorned with every accomplishment, is most distinguished among all royal dynasties. Joy in the happiness of others, grief at sight of other people's misery, desire to alleviate distress, abstention from injury, sincerity, forgiveness, and truth,--these... prevail amongst the Kurus... it would be a pity if anything improper were done by any one belonging to it, and greater pity still if it were done by thee. O chief of the Kurus, thou art the first of those that should restrain the Kurus if they behave deceitfully towards strangers or those numbering with themselves.'

statements.claim: Krishna told Dhritarashtra his wicked sons, headed by Duryodhana, abandoning both virtue and profit, disregarding morality and deprived of their senses by avarice, were acting most unrighteously toward their foremost of kinsmen; the terrible danger had its origin in the conduct of the Kurus, and if he became indifferent it would produce universal slaughter, but if willing he might allay the danger even yet, for peace was not difficult of acquisition.
statements.evidence: MBh 5.095: 'those wicked sons of thine, headed by Duryodhana, abandoning both virtue and profit, disregarding morality, and deprived of their senses by avarice, are now acting most unrighteously towards... their foremost of kinsmen. That terrible danger (which threatens all) hath its origin in the conduct of the Kurus. If thou becomest indifferent to it, it will then produce a universal slaughter. If... thou art willing, thou mayest be able to allay that danger even yet, for... peace, I think, is not difficult of acquisition.'

statements.claim: The establishment of peace depended on the king and Krishna himself: 'Set right your sons, O king, and I will set the Pandavas right.' Whatever the king commanded his sons with their followers should obey; living in obedience to him would be the very best they could do; striving for peace by restraining his sons would profit him and benefit the Pandavas; and protected by the illustrious sons of Pandu, Indra himself at the head of the celestials would not be able to vanquish him, much less mere earthly kings.
statements.evidence: MBh 5.095: 'The establishment of peace, O king, depends on thee and myself, O monarch. Set right thy sons... and I will set the Pandavas right. Whatever be thy command, O king, it behoveth thy sons with their followers to obey it... If thou strivest for peace by restraining thy sons, it will be to thy profit... as also to the benefit of the Pandavas... Protected by the illustrious sons of Pandu, Indra himself at the head of the celestials will not be able to vanquish thee. How would it be possible then for mere earthly kings to withstand thy prowess?'

statements.claim: With Bhishma, Drona, Kripa, Karna, Aswatthaman, Vikarna, Somadatta, Vahlika, the chief of the Sindhus, the ruler of the Kalingas and Sudakshina of the Kamvojas on one side, and Yudhishthira, Bhimasena, Savyasachin, the twins, Satyaki and Yuyutsu on the other, only a man of misdirected intelligence would fight such a host.
statements.evidence: MBh 5.095: 'If with Bhishma, and Drona, and Kripa, and Karna, and Vivinsati, and Aswatthaman, Vikarna, and Somadatta, and Vahlika and the chief of the Sindhus, and the ruler of the Kalingas, and Sudakshina, the king of the Kamvojas, there were Yudhishthira, and Bhimasena and Savyasachin, and the twins, and if Satyaki of mighty energy, and Yuyutsu, that mighty car warrior, are stationed, who is there... of such misdirected intelligence that would fight these?' (Story's roster matches; it simply does not repeat Vivinsati.)

statements.claim: With both the Kurus and the Pandavas at his back, the sovereignty of the whole world and invincibility before all foes would be Dhritarashtra's; all the rulers of the earth would seek alliance with him, and protected by sons, grandsons, fathers, brothers and friends he would live in exceeding happiness.
statements.evidence: MBh 5.095: 'If... thou hast both the Kurus and the Pandavas at thy back, the sovereignty of the whole world and invincibility before all foes will be thine. All the rulers of the earth... will then seek alliance with thee. Protected on all sides by sons, grandsons, fathers, brothers, and friends, thou wilt then be able to live in exceeding happiness.'

statements.claim: In battle nothing but wholesale destruction was visible; in the destruction of both parties there was no merit; whether the Pandavas were slaughtered or his own mighty sons fell, no happiness would remain; all of them — Pandavas and his sons alike — were brave, skilled in weapons and desirous of battle; after the battle he would not behold all the Kurus or all the Pandavas, and car-warriors slain by car-warriors, the heroes of both parties would be reduced in numbers and strength.
statements.evidence: MBh 5.095: 'In battle, O great king, nothing but wholesale destruction is visible. Indeed, in the destruction of both the parties, what merit dost thou see? If the Pandavas are slaughtered in battle, or if thy own mighty sons fall, tell me... what happiness wilt thou enjoy? All of them are brave and skilled in weapons. All of them are desirous of battle, the Pandavas as also thy sons. Oh, save them from the terrible danger that threatens them. After the battle thou wilt not behold all the Kurus or all the Pandavas. Car-warriors slain by car-warriors, thou wilt behold the heroes of both parties reduced in numbers and strength.'

statements.claim: All the rulers of the earth had been assembled, and inflamed with wrath they would not stop short of destroying one another.
statements.evidence: MBh 5.095: 'All the rulers of the earth... have been assembled together. Inflamed with wrath, they will certainly exte[rminate each other]' (passage truncates at this point; the continuation is consistent with the story's rendering, and the pack excerpt's 'Save, O king, the world' theme supports the warning of wholesale mutual destruction).

statements.claim: Closing frame: Krishna had laid before the blind king the whole arithmetic of war — every warrior counted, every alliance weighed — and the choice was plainly Dhritarashtra's to make.
statements.evidence: Non-factual summation of the alternatives Krishna set out in 5.095; the 'blind king' is the canonical epithet used throughout the source.

notes: Direct rendering of MBh 5.095's assembly speech, including the two-sided roster of champions and the destruction imagery. The pack's own excerpt confirms the surrounding appeal ('Save, O king, the world... Giving unto the Pandavas their just share of the paternal kingdom').

statements.claim: When Krishna finished speaking, all who sat in the assembly remained silent, their hair standing on end, and all the kings thought there was no man who could dare reply to that speech.
statements.evidence: MBh 5.096: 'Hearing these words uttered by the high-souled Kesava, all the persons who sat in that assembly remained silent, their hair standing on their ends. And all the kings thought within themselves that there was no man who could dare reply to that speech.'

statements.claim: Seeing the kings silent, Jamadagni's son Parashurama addressed Duryodhana in that assembly, saying: 'Listen confidingly to my words illustrated by an example, and seek thy own good if my speech recommends itself to thee.'
statements.evidence: MBh 5.096: 'seeing that all the kings sat silent, Jamadagni's son (addressing Duryodhana) then said these words in that assembly of Kurus, Listen confidingly to my words illustrated by an example, and seek thy own good if my speech recommends itself to thee.'

statements.claim: There was a king of yore named Dambhodbhava, who was the Head of the earth and whose sovereignty extended over the whole world; rising every morning after the night had passed, that mighty car-warrior called the Brahmanas and Kshatriyas and asked whether any one — Sudra, Vaisya, Kshatriya or Brahmana — was superior or even equal to him in battle, and uttering those words he wandered over the earth, intoxicated with pride and thinking of nothing else.
statements.evidence: MBh 5.096: 'There was a king of yore named Dambhodbhava, who was the Head of the earth... his sovereignty extended over the whole world. And that mighty car-warrior, rising every morning after the night had passed away, called the Brahmanas and the Kshatriyas unto himself and asked them... Be he a Sudra, a Vaisya, a Kshatriya, or a Brahmana, is there any one who is superior or even equal to me in battle?... And uttering these words that king wandered over the earth, intoxicated with pride and thinking of nothing else.'

statements.claim: High-souled Brahmanas, conversant with the Vedas and fearing nothing on earth, counselled the monarch to curb his pride, but though forbidden he went on asking the same question day after day; at last Brahmanas endued with ascetic merit and inflamed with anger told him that two persons, foremost of all men and always victorious in battle, existed whom he could by no means equal if he sought an encounter with either.
statements.evidence: MBh 5.096: 'certain Brahmanas endued with high souls, conversant with the Vedas, and fearing nothing on earth, counselled the monarch... to curb his pride. But though forbidden by those Brahmanas to boast in that way, the king continued to ask... the same question day after day. And some high-souled Brahmanas then, endued with ascetic merit... were inflamed with anger... There are two persons who are foremost of all men and who are always victorious in battle. Thou, O king, wilt by no means be equal to them if thou seekest an encounter with any one of them.'

statements.claim: The king asked where the two heroes were to be found, in what race born and what feats achieved; the Brahmanas answered that they were ascetics called Nara and Narayana, both born in the race of man, then practising the severest penances in a hidden region of the mountains of Gandhamadana.
statements.evidence: MBh 5.096: 'Where may those two heroes be found? In what race are they born? What feats have they achieved?... those two persons are ascetics called Nara and Narayana. They have both taken their births in the race of man... It is that illustrious pair, Nara and Narayana, who are now practising the severest of penances in some hidden region of the mountains of Gandhamadana.'

statements.claim: Unable to bear even their reputation, the king speedily mustered his large army of the six kinds of forces and marched to the rugged and frightful mountains of Gandhamadana, where he searched the woods and came upon the two ascetics concealed within them, emaciated with hunger and thirst, their veins swollen and visible, much afflicted by cold winds and the hot rays of the sun.
statements.evidence: MBh 5.096: 'that king speedily mustered his large army consisting of six kinds of forces, and unable to bear their reputation, marched to the spot where those unvanquished ascetics were, and arrived at the rugged and frightful mountains of Gandhamadana. He began to search after those Rishis, and at last, came upon them concealed within the woods. And beholding those two best of persons emaciated with hunger and thirst, their veins swollen and visible, and themselves much afflicted with cold winds, and the hot rays of the sun...'

statements.claim: The king approached the Rishis, touched their feet and enquired after their welfare; they received him hospitably with fruits and roots, a seat and water, asked his business and said 'Let it be done.'
statements.evidence: MBh 5.096: 'he approached them, and touching their feet, enquired after their welfare. And the two Rishis received the king hospitably, with fruits and roots, and a seat and water. And they then enquired after the king's business, saying, Let it be done.'

statements.claim: The king spoke his customary words: 'The whole earth has been conquered by the might of my arms. All my foes have been slain. Desiring a battle with you both I have come to this mountain. Offer me this hospitality. I have been cherishing this wish from a long time.'
statements.evidence: MBh 5.096: 'the king said unto them the same words that he was in the habit of saying unto all... The whole earth has been conquered by the might of my arms. All my foes have been slain. Desiring a battle with you both I have come to this mountain. Offer me this hospitality. I have been cherishing this wish from a long time.'

statements.claim: Nara and Narayana replied that wrath and covetousness had no place in that retreat, no battle was possible there, there were no weapons and nothing of unrighteousness and malice, and he should seek battle elsewhere, for there were many Kshatriyas on earth.
statements.evidence: MBh 5.096: 'wrath and covetousness have no place in this retreat. How can a battle, therefore, be possible here? There are no weapons here, and nothing of unrighteousness and malice. Seek battle elsewhere. There are many Kshatriyas on earth.'

statements.claim: The king still pressed them; the Rishis continually soothed him and overlooked his importunity, but Dambhodbhava repeatedly summoned them to fight, until Nara took up a handful of grass-blades and said, 'Desirous of battle as thou art, come, O Kshatriya, and fight! Take up all thy arms, and array thy troops. I will curb thy eagerness for battle hereafter!'
statements.evidence: MBh 5.096: 'Although thus addressed, the king still pressed them for giving him battle. The Rishis, however, continually soothed him and overlooked his importunity. King Dambhodbhava, still desirous of battle, repeatedly summoned those Rishis to fight. Nara, then... taking up a handful of grass-blades, said... Desirous of battle as thou art, come, O Kshatriya, and fight! Take up all thy arms, and array thy troops. I will curb thy eagerness for battle hereafter!'

statements.claim: Dambhodbhava answered he had come desiring to fight and would fight even against such a weapon; with all his troops he covered every side with a shower of arrows, but the ascetic, by means of the blades of grass, baffled all those terrible shafts capable of mangling the bodies of hostile warriors; the invincible Rishi then let off his own terrible weapon made of grass-blades, incapable of being counteracted, and what followed was highly wonderful.
statements.evidence: MBh 5.096: 'Dambhodbhava then said... I have come hither desirous of fighting. Saying this, Dambhodbhava with all his troops, desirous of slaying that ascetic, covered all sides with a shower of arrows. That ascetic, however, by means of those blades of grass, baffled all those terrible shafts of the king that were capable of mangling the bodies of hostile warriors. The invincible Rishi then let off towards the king his own terrible weapon made of grass-blades and which was incapable of being counteracted. And highly wonderful was that which happ[ened]...' (pack passage truncates; the story's 'silenced every boast' close is narrative colour consistent with the defeat of the boastful king).

statements.claim: Parashurama delivered the point: 'They that were Nara and Narayana in days of yore are now Arjuna and Kesava. Know then, O great king, who these brave and foremost of persons are. If thou believest in this and dost not mistrust me adopt thou a virtuous resolution and make peace with the sons of Pandu.'
statements.evidence: Pack excerpt (5.096): 'Rama continued... They that were Nara and Narayana in days of yore are now Arjuna and Kesava. Know then, O great king, who those brave and foremost of persons are. If thou believest in this and dost not mistrust me adopt thou a virtuous resolution and make peace with the sons of Pandu.'

statements.claim: Closing frame: the kings of the earth looked at the two men among them — the charioteer-brother and the prince who had come to plead — and heard the oldest names in the world laid over their newest faces.
statements.evidence: Poetic close referencing the Nara-Narayana = Krishna-Arjuna identification just announced by Parashurama. Note: only Krishna (with Vidura and Satyaki) physically entered the assembly per 5.094; Arjuna was with the Pandavas, so the pairing here is rhetorical — identifying Krishna with the ancient pair — rather than a claim that Arjuna was present in the court.

notes: The embedded Dambhodbhava tale is rendered faithfully from MBh 5.096; quotes track the Ganguli text closely. Only Arjuna's physical presence at the assembly is arguably implied by the closing metaphor — treated as connective, since 5.094 shows only Krishna entering the court.
